transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-03-03 15:00 UTC | Duration ~45m | Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Raman (Redwood SE), Samir Patel (Redwood SE), Alex Nguyen (BuildCo Backend), Mei Chen (BuildCo SRE), Carlos Ruiz (BuildCo PM), Taylor Park (BuildCo ML)

Summary (auto): Weekly check-in for the POC. Focused on latency tuning - TTFT regression observed in production-like traces, streaming behavior, sequence length distribution effects, and kernel selection. Action items captured.

[00:00] Jordan: All right everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call, and then Priya will walk through the bench results we ran last week.
[00:10] Alex: hey, yep, I'm here.
[00:12] Mei: here.
[00:13] Carlos: here.
[00:15] Taylor: present.
[00:18] Priya: cool, I'll share my screen in a sec. So the headline: TTFT is still about 30-40ms higher on your workloads versus our internal baseline when streaming is on.
[00:29] Alex: hmm that tracks with what we saw, our user metrics spiked for first response time after we started using longer prompts.
[00:35] Priya: right, and we instrumented microbenchmarks: 1) cold-start resps with empty KV cache 2) warm with prefix caching 3) streaming enabled vs chunked non-streaming.
[00:46] Samir: one quick note, some of our kernel variants show better token-start latency but slightly worse sustained throughput; tradeoff there.
[00:56] Priya: exactly. So the specific numbers: for 512-seq with streaming on, TTFT measured ~160ms on your trace vs ~125ms internal. For 2048-seq it jumps to ~230ms vs ~180ms. Those are median numbers, 95th is higher.
[01:18] Taylor: are these with quantized kernels or FP16?
[01:21] Priya: these were int8 quantized kernels (q4 variant) because that's what you selected for cost reasons. We also ran an fp16 baseline — FP16 reduces TTFT by ~15-25ms but increases per-token cost.
[01:33] Mei: do we know where the extra time is coming from? network? kernel init?
[01:37] Priya: dig into the flamegraphs, it's a mix: 1) kernel dispatch overhead for small batch sizes 2) streaming framing + protobuf serialization 3) attention kv cache lookup overhead for long sequences.
[01:49] Alex: the streaming framing — can we optimize chunk size? we send every 64 tokens now.
[01:53] Priya: yes chunk size matters. smaller chunks increase TTFT because more round trips; larger chunks increase first token latency but reduce total overhead. There's a sweet spot at ~128 tokens for your traces, but it depends.
[02:05] Jordan: can you explain the continuous batching/affinity we talked about last week? does that affect TTFT?
[02:10] Samir: continuous batching helps throughput but can increase first-token latency if we're waiting to fill a micro-batch; our runtime prioritizes immediate dispatch for low-latency routes but if you route through cheaper pools we see wait time.
[02:22] Carlos: so that's policy tuning? like route to dedicated cold pool vs hosted low-cost?
[02:26] Priya: yes. For the POC we recommended using dedicated nodes for your high-priority route to reduce scheduling jitter. That eliminates queueing but costs more.
[02:35] Taylor: any impact from model sharding or kernel choices? you mentioned kernel A vs B.
[02:40] Priya: kernel A (new attention-fused kernel) has lower per-token latency for long sequences but slightly higher startup overhead; kernel B (legacy optimized) is quicker for TTFT on short sequences. So for 512 sequence kernel B looked better; for 2048 kernel A wins.
[02:57] Alex: are those kernels per model or per runtime? can we toggle per-route?
[03:01] Priya: runtime-level selection, but we can expose it as a model variant in the POC so you can route different routes to different kernel profiles.
[03:10] Mei: what about KV cache warming? does prefix caching help?
[03:14] Samir: yes if you have repeated prompts/prefixes we can cache the KV state and reduce the token compute for subsequent calls. But the first call still pays the full cost. We saw about 25% less compute for warmed prefixes in your dataset.
[03:28] Alex: our main issue is TTFT on brand new prompts from users though, so caching helps only a bit.
[03:33] Priya: so we proposed a few knobs: 1) try FP16 kernel for hot routes 2) tune streaming chunk size from 64 -> 128 3) route high-priority flows to Dedicated pool with pre-warmed workers 4) experiment with kernel A/B split by sequence length via routing rules.
[03:51] Carlos: what's the delta on cost if we move hot flux to Dedicated?
[03:55] Jordan: we'll send you pricing but ballpark Dedicated reserved capacity is higher fixed cost but lowers per-token latency and avoids noisy neighbor interference; for the pilot we can provision a small pool to validate.
[04:06] Taylor: and how about our sequence length distribution — we saw a tail up to 3500 tokens for rare cases, is that a big problem?
[04:13] Priya: very long sequences push KV memory usage and select different kernels; we recommend capping streaming chunking for tails and optionally truncating or summarizing long contexts before inference.
[04:23] Mei: network-wise we also have tighter egress limits. would Dedicated VPC peering help?
[04:28] Samir: yes VPC peering and colocating reduces network jitter; we'll ask for your egress numbers.
[04:33] Alex: we already uploaded a sample of 500 prompts in the drive, we'll add longer tails.
[04:37] Jordan: perfect. Priya, what are the bench tasks you're going to run this week?
[04:40] Priya: run A/B kernel bench: kernel A vs B with quantized and FP16 variants for seq lengths [512, 1024, 2048], streaming enabled with chunk sizes [64, 128], and with both cold-start and warmed KV cache. We'll capture median and P95 TTFT and per-token throughput.
[04:58] Carlos: timeline?
[05:00] Priya: aim to have raw results by Friday (2026-03-06). We'll share a spreadsheet with latencies and cost estimates for each config.
[05:08] Alex: can you also show the percent of requests that hit the warmed cache in your warm run?
[05:12] Samir: yes we'll include hit-rate metrics.
[05:15] Taylor: any quick wins we can do on our side?
[05:18] Priya: yes: 1) increase initial chunk size to 128 for streaming 2) enforce soft truncation for >3000 tokens with a summarization step 3) reduce client-side small-batch aggregation — send slightly larger batches when latency SLO allows.
[05:33] Mei: uncertain about truncation - some customers rely on full context; will need to check product tradeoffs.
[05:37] Carlos: we'll discuss internal requirements and report back.
[05:40] Jordan: security ask: BuildCo wanted SOC2 and audit logs; I'll send the docs.
[05:44] Alex: thanks. Also can you share kernel docs or short note on what kernel A/B are doing? the naming was a bit fuzzy in last deck.
[05:52] Priya: sure, we'll include an appendix describing kernel differences, typical wins/losses, and the quantization tradeoffs (int8 vs fp16).
[06:00] Jordan: any competitors come up in your evaluation?
[06:03] Carlos: we looked at Triton as an internal experiment and briefly at Anthropic for model quality. Pricing with OpenAI was off the chart for our volume.
[06:12] Priya: noted. We'll try to include comparative throughput numbers where possible but this POC focuses on tuning our runtime.
[06:18] Alex: last question — what does the Dedicated pilot look like operationally? zero-downtime? SLA?
[06:24] Jordan: for pilot we typically provision a small Dedicated pool with pre-warmed workers and a testing route; SLA during pilot is advisory but we can put in place monitoring and rollback to hosted. For production Dedicated has SLA options.
[06:38] Mei: fine. we'll need details on peering and certs.
[06:41] Jordan: I'll add that to next steps.
[06:44] Priya: ok to recap actions? We'll run kernel A/B + streaming variants, share results Friday, Jordan will send pricing and SOC2, BuildCo to upload full prompt set and confirm SLOs.
[06:57] Carlos: yep that's right.
[06:59] Alex: thanks everyone.
[07:01] Jordan: thanks all. We'll follow up in the shared doc and schedule the Dedicated pilot slot for next week pending bench results.

Notes/Artifacts shared: bench spreadsheet (link: drive.buildco/bench-2026-03-03), POC runbook (link: redwood/poc/runbook), SOC2 security packet (to be shared).

End of transcript.
